samples.text:
Nowadays people can find almost any information on the internet with their phones or computers. For this reason, some people think that public libraries are not necessary any more. I strongly disagree with this opinion.

Firstly, not everyone has access to the internet at home. Some families are poor and they cannot pay for a computer or a good internet connection. For these people, the library is the only place where they can use computers for free, search for jobs or do their homework. If libraries are closed, this people will have fewer chance to improve their life.

Secondly, libraries are not only a place for books. They are also a quiet place for students to study, especially for those who live in small houses with big families. In my city, the library is always full of university students during exam period, because they can concentrate there better than at home. Also, libraries organise many activities like reading clubs for children, language classes and events for old people. These activities help people to meet each other and feel part of the community.

Thirdly, not all information on the internet is reliable. There are many fake news and wrong information online. In the library, the books are chosen carefully and librarians can help people to find good sources for their research.

Some people say that libraries cost a lot of money for the government. But I think this money is a good investment because libraries give education and support to everyone.

In conclusion, I disagree that public libraries are no longer necessary. Even though a lot of information is online, libraries still provide free access, a place to study and community activities, so we should keep them.

samples.text:
With the vast amount of information now available online, some people claim that public libraries have become unnecessary. I strongly disagree with this view, as libraries provide important services that the internet cannot replace.

Firstly, libraries play a crucial role in providing equal access to information. Although internet use is widespread, a significant number of people still lack a reliable connection or a suitable device at home, particularly the elderly people and low-income families. For them, the local library offers free computers, printing and Wi-Fi, allowing them to apply for jobs, access government services and complete school assignments. Without libraries, the gap between those who are connected and those who are not would likely widen.

Secondly, the internet contains a great deal of information, but much of it is inaccurate or misleading. Librarians are trained to help people find reliable sources and to evaluate what they read, which is an increasingly valuable skill in the age of misinformation. Libraries also give free access to books, academic journals and databases that would otherwise be expensive, which benefits students and researchers alike.

In addition, libraries serve as community spaces. They offer a quiet environment for studying, host activities such as story sessions for young children and digital skills classes for older adults, and provide a safe, welcoming place for people to meet. In an era where many people feel isolated, these functions are arguably more important than ever.

Admittedly, libraries need to adapt to changing habits, for example by expanding their digital collections and offering more flexible opening hours. However, this is a reason to modernise them, not to close them.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that public libraries remain necessary despite the growth of online information. They ensure fair access to knowledge, support reliable research and strengthen local communities in ways the internet cannot.

samples.text:
The claim that public libraries have been rendered obsolete by the internet rests on the assumption that their sole purpose is to supply information. I disagree with this view. While the internet has undoubtedly changed how people find information, libraries continue to fulfil social, educational and democratic functions that online resources cannot replicate.

Perhaps the most important of these is ensuring equal access. It is easy to assume that everyone is online, yet many households still lack a reliable connection, an adequate device or the skills needed to use them effectively. As more essential services, from job applications to benefit claims, move online, a library's free computers and trained staff become a lifeline for those at risk of being left behind. Closing libraries would therefore deepen existing inequalities at the very moment when digital participation has become essential.

Libraries also address a problem the internet has intensified rather than solved: the difficulty of distinguishing reliable information from falsehood. Librarians guide users towards credible sources and help them develop the critical skills to evaluate what they read. Moreover, much high-quality content, including many academic journals and recent books, remains behind paywalls, and libraries make it freely available to anyone.

Beyond information, libraries function as some of the few remaining public spaces that are open to everyone and require no payment. Students without a quiet place to study at home, parents attending reading sessions with toddlers and older people seeking company all rely on them. In an increasingly fragmented society, such shared spaces help sustain a sense of community.

This is not to suggest that libraries should remain unchanged. They must continue to evolve, expanding digital lending and offering training in technology. But adaptation is an argument for investment, not closure.

In conclusion, public libraries remain necessary because their value extends far beyond information retrieval, encompassing equality of access, digital literacy and community life.
